text: Every qubit state can be written in infinitely many equivalent bases, but one of them gets used by default everywhere. This lesson is about that one basis — and about the fact that it's a choice, not the only option.

The set ket-zero, ket-one is called the computational basis because it's the basis a quantum processor's final measurement physically reports in — hardware is built to return one of two outcomes, conventionally labeled 0 and 1. Every circuit diagram and every bitstring a program returns uses this basis by default. It isn't mathematically special in any deeper sense — it's just the one hardware and tooling standardized on.

A commonly used alternative is the X-basis: ket-plus equals ket-zero plus ket-one over root 2, and ket-minus equals ket-zero minus ket-one over root 2. Both are normalized — one over root 2, squared, twice, gives 0.5 plus 0.5, exactly 1 — and they're orthogonal to each other. So this pair is every bit as valid a basis as the computational one; it's just a different pair of directions to measure along.

The relationship works both ways: ket-zero equals ket-plus plus ket-minus over root 2, and ket-one equals ket-plus minus ket-minus over root 2. Any state in this space can be expressed in either basis — switching between them is just a change of coordinates, exactly like changing basis for an ordinary vector. Nothing about the physical qubit changes when you describe it one way instead of the other.

Here's the subtlety that makes this more than notation: which basis you measure in determines what 'the outcome' even means. A state that looks perfectly definite in one basis, like ket-zero, gives an even 50/50 split when measured in the X-basis — Chapter 3 works through this precisely. Quantum algorithms exploit exactly this: they rotate a qubit into a different basis mid-circuit, using gates like Hadamard, so interference lines up correctly, then rotate back into the computational basis right before the final measurement, because that's the basis hardware actually reads out.
Next lesson goes deeper on normalization itself — why the rule is forced rather than a convention, and a strange fact called global phase.
